linkages: All household members in the Danish Expenditure Survey are linked to official Danish registries through their social security number
Parents are linked to their children through the parent-child links contained in the population-wide Danish registries
Self-reported consumption in the survey is linked to registry proxies to estimate the imputation model (Equation 9), which is then applied to all households

sample.universe: Danish residents: pairs of parents and children, and households participating in the Danish Expenditure Survey 1995-2009
sample.unit_of_observation: Pair of one parent and one child (mobility regressions); household (imputation sample and Table 4)
selection_rules: Imputation sample: households that participated in the DES between 1995 and 2009 in which the head of the household was between 25 and 74 years old (3,297 single and 5,278 married households)
Consumption sample: pairs of parents and children in which the parent participated in the DES between 1995 and 2009
Consumption sample: the parent was at least 40 years old in 1995
Consumption sample: the parent was no more than 74 years old in 2009
Consumption sample: the child was at least 25 years old in 1995
Income sample: the same age requirements, but no requirement that the parent participated in the DES; selected from the entire Danish population
sample.period: 1980-2009 (earnings and income of parents 1980-1989; consumption, earnings and income of children 1995-2009; wealth in 2010 for Table 4)
sample.n_observations: 1,690 parent-child pairs (consumption sample); 231,011 parent-child pairs (income sample); 8,351 observations for the expenditure-income ratio and 46,546 for the wealth-income ratio in Table 4
sample.n_individuals: Consumption sample: 720 fathers and 970 mothers, 735 sons and 955 daughters. Income sample: 105,600 fathers and 125,411 mothers, 107,662 sons and 123,349 daughters

construction_notes: Household expenditures are approximated as x ≈ y − Δw, disposable income minus the change in household wealth (Equation 1, following Browning & Leth-Petersen, 2003)

Log permanent consumption is defined as average log consumption over the 15 years 1995-2009 (Equation 3); 'permanent consumption' means time-averaged consumption and does not refer to the probabilistic properties of household consumption

Consumption is imputed by regressing log self-reported consumption on registry proxies and demographic variables (Equation 9), estimated by 2SLS instrumenting total expenditures and the home value with 2-year lagged total expenditures, mean total expenditures by gender and three-digit occupation, mean home values by gender and three-digit occupation, and mean home values by zip code
Equation 9 is estimated separately for singles (observations pooled over three consecutive years with year dummies) and for couples (one regression per year)
An equivalence scale for couples equal to the square root of two is applied, and each spouse is assigned half of the couple's total consumption
On average, the housing imputation model explains 76% of the total variation in the market prices of houses and condominiums within each year from 1995 to 2009
Estimated with OLS, the imputation model (Equation 9) explains an average of 35% of the variation in self-reported consumption within each year
Earnings and income of parents are measured over 1980-1989, because many parents have retired by 1995-2009; 1980 is the first year with earnings and income data in the Danish registries

Standard errors: robust asymptotic in the income sample; bootstrapped in the consumption sample, with 200 draws replicating the whole estimation process including the imputation of housing values, the imputation of consumption in each year, the construction of permanent consumption and the final estimation
When testing the equality of two regression coefficients, a nonzero sample correlation between the coefficients is allowed for
For Table 4, the present value of permanent disposable income is computed with an annual interest rate of 2%

claims.statement: The intergenerational elasticity of individual after-tax earnings in Denmark, estimated in the consumption sample, is 0.086: a 1% higher log time-averaged parent after-tax earnings is associated with a 0.086% higher log time-averaged child after-tax earnings.

treatment.label: Log parent time-averaged (permanent) individual after-tax earnings

definition.value: The log of the parent's individual after-tax earnings, time-averaged over the 10-year period 1980-1989. The paper measures parent earnings in 1980-1989 rather than 1995-2009 because many parents have retired by the later period; 1980 is the first year with earnings data in the Danish registries.

timing.value: Averaged over 1980-1989, when the parents are 39-48 years old on average

outcome.label: Log child time-averaged (permanent) individual after-tax earnings

definition.value: The log of the child's individual after-tax earnings, time-averaged over the sample period. The dependent variable in all Table 2 regressions is the log child outcome.

timing.value: Time-averaged over the sample period, when the children are 30-44 years old on average

units.value: elasticity: log points of child after-tax earnings per log point of parent after-tax earnings

magnitude.interpretation: the intergenerational elasticity of individual time-averaged earnings in Denmark is approximately 0.05–0.10

estimand.target_population: Pairs of Danish parents and children satisfying the age requirements, in the consumption sample

population.description: Pairs of parents and children in which the parent participated in the Danish Expenditure Survey between 1995 and 2009 (the 'consumption sample'), 1,690 parent-child pairs

identification.source_of_variation: No policy or natural experiment: the parent's time-averaged after-tax earnings is instrumented with the mean earnings in Denmark by gender and three-digit occupational code, in order to remove attenuation bias from measurement error in parent earnings.

key_assumptions.assumption: The error term in the mobility regression has mean zero and is uncorrelated with the independent variables of the model, the parent outcome and the demographic controls Di

rhs: 𝜀i (unobserved determinants of child after-tax earnings)

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: the mean earnings in Denmark by gender and three-digit occupational code predicts the parent's time-averaged after-tax earnings

implies_edges.from: Mean earnings in Denmark by gender and three-digit occupational code

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: the gender-by-occupation mean earnings instrument affects the child's earnings only through the parent's time-averaged after-tax earnings (and the controls Di)

implies_edges.from: Mean earnings in Denmark by gender and three-digit occupational code

key_assumptions.assumption: Life-cycle bias is small: because parent and child earnings are measured at a fairly similar age, the downward bias in the estimated persistence of earnings is likely to be small
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 mean ages (parents 39-48, children 30-44 / 29-43) and the arguments of Grawe (2006) and Haider and Solon (2006)

threats_discussed: Life-cycle bias: households with higher lifetime earnings have steeper age-earnings profiles, so measuring parent and child earnings at different ages biases the estimated persistence downwards (Grawe, 2006; Haider & Solon, 2006)
Attenuation bias from measurement error in parental earnings, addressed by 2SLS
robustness_checks: Estimation in two independent samples: the consumption sample (1,690 pairs) and the income sample (231,011 pairs)
unresolved_confounders: A small remaining downward bias in the estimated persistence of earnings from measuring parent and child earnings at different stages of the life cycle
